Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) and the hon. member for Joli-ette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), I say without the slightest hesitation that the hon. member for Sherbrooke has contributed to this debate in a much more serious fashion than the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm at the outset condemned what the hon. member for Sherbrooke had said.
He said that if things go on as they are, Canada will be marking its centenary as a colony in 1967; the mere mention of that fact is ridiculous. Moreover, he spent his time talking first about two flags, then about six flags, stating that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had favoured two flags.
It is evident to anyone who takes a serious look at the situation that the Leader of the Opposition spoke of one national flag; but he added that the union jack could be kept for those who wish to use it occasionally. Besides, we have seen and we still see every day in the province of Quebec, on our national day or in Corpus Christi processions, people who, after having been detached from France for more than 200 years, still display the blue, white and red flag of France, which is very decorative. That does not mean however that they are more French than Canadian. This simply means they still keep in their hearts a certain feeling for their old mother country.
I must say I have admired the speech of the hon. member for Sherbrooke. But I must disagree with my colleague from Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), because I do not share all his views. I rather regret that purely political motives should have been included in this matter, as was done most particularly by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm.
I suggest that this matter should be dealt with objectively, as was done by the hon. member for Sherbrooke, whom I congratulate.
We can hold different views. We can claim that it should be up to the government to rule on the matter, especially since it has been under discussion for many years. But, on the other hand, I do not object to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke that we should ask a committee formed of persons having some particular knowledge of the arts, to choose among the thousands of designs

which have been submitted to us, and which are still being continuously submitted to us, the one which best represents the aspirations of the whole of Canada.
As all hon. members probably did, I presume, I recently received some suggestions. These suggestions dealt with four acceptable flag designs. First, there was a distinctive national flag; a red flag with a gilded maple leaf and ten gilded bars representing the ten provinces; this would be the Canadian flag. There would also be a flag for the navy, a red maple leaf on a white field, with ten red bars representing the ten provinces of Canada. There would also be a flag for the Department of Transport, a gilded maple leaf on a blue field with ten gilded bars representing the ten provinces of Canada. Finally, there would be a flag for the merchant navy: a green maple leaf on a white field, with ten green bars representing the various provinces of Canada. Nobody can raise objections to those four proposals because they have a special meaning since they represent for Canada: the merchant marine, the Department of Transport and Canada's navy.
Those are suggestions that might be submitted to a committee having made studies and with special knowledge in the field of aesthetics.
This measure contains the interesting provision that the members of that committee must within a period of one year, report to parliament on their research and findings.
It must be kept in mind that the final decision rests with parliament or the government. I think that the suggestion should come from the government. The government should be the one to decide and submit a bill to parliament which, in turn, would finally adopt it.
Besides, I do not believe it is essential that the government submit such a bill. It can take a decision, as was done before in the case of the Canadian flag floating over our embassies, the red flag with a union jack in a corner and the arms of Canada. That was decided by order in council just the same as the Quebec provincial government adopted its own flag by order in council. It submitted a flag and said: This is the flag of the province of Quebec. That is what the government of that province has decided. That government took the responsibility. Whether you like it or not, it is the recognized flag of the province of Quebec.
In my opinion, this idea of referring the question to a committee such as the Canada Council for examination, is a good one and I am all for it.
Canadian Sovereignty
I was interested in the historical account given by the hon. member for Sherbrooke. The signing of the treaty of Westminster in 1931 was the crowing achievement of a series of steps taken since 1760 towards the full independence of Canada. There was the Quebec Act, the constitutional regime, the Act of Union, confederation and finally, the Statute of Westminster.
We have seen that our heads of state had started to establish Canada's position long before that. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier was invited to Queen Victoria's diamond jubilee, in 1897, he made moves, over there, backed by General Smuts of South Africa, in favour of greater independence for the dominions within the commonwealth.
Then, in 1919, Sir Robert Borden, as Prime Minister, insisted, as the member for Sherbrooke said, that Canada be called upon to sign the Versailles peace treaty in its own name, because our troops had fought as a Canadian unit, not as part of the British forces.
In 1926, the Canadian people stood up against a governor general who intervened in the political affairs of our country and who was immediately recalled. From that moment, there was much talk about the treaty of Westminster. The Hon. Ernest Lapointe signed the fisheries agreement with the United States, but refused to do so in the presence of Great Britain's representative, thus indicating that Canada intended to become completely autonomous. Thereafter, from 1927 to 1930, the various dominions set up the basis for the Westminster treaty, which was signed on the 11th of December, 1931.
Therefore, I see no objection to the three projects being grouped in one, since they all tend to a full and complete autonomy for Canada.
That is why I commend the hon. member for Sherbrooke. I commend him for the moderation of his remarks. I think we should discuss those national matters in a non-partisan way. We should discuss them with the broadness of mind of Canadians who want to be Canadians.
We have no right to condemn the Englishspeaking Canadians who have not yet attained the same degree of national maturity as the French-speaking Canadians, because many of them still have relatives overseas-brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, grandfathers, grandmothers-and they still have in their heart some feeling for England.
But it should not be overlooked that the union jack is made up of three crosses: Saint George's cross, standing for England, Saint Andrew's cross, standing for Scotland, and Saint Patrick's cross, standing for Ireland. These three countries together form what we

Canadian Sovereignty
consider today not England but the United Kingdom. No, the union jack has no connection whatsoever with Canada.
We must respect the union jack because it is the emblem under which we enjoyed a great measure of protection. We must respect it in the same way as we, French-Canadians, respect the French flag, which represents something for us. However, to respect it does not mean to brandish it at every occasion as the sole guide to our conduct.
We must have a distinctive Canadian flag bearing neither the union jack nor the fleur-de-lis because the union jack represents England and the countries around it, while the fleur-de-lis is an old relic from France which can certainly be cast off. There has been talk about the national anthem. Last Sunday, following the victory of the Canadian team over the American team, the band started playing "O Canada". While listening to it, I was proud of the fact that, in other countries, "O Canada" was recognized as our national anthem. I admit that some people do not like "O Canada"; they may be right, because it is often badly sung and badly played. In fact, in some circles, it is often sung like a funeral dirge, when it should be possible to underline its real beauty. Among the bands that play it very well, the R.C.A.F. band and the governor general's band give it a vigorous and martial flavour that really represents this young country of ours. Played in such a way, "O Canada" is truly beautiful. In our schools, we should teach our children to sing ''O Canada" with ardour, so that it may be a true demonstration of the Canadian spirit.
Mr. Speaker, I approve the bill because it sets a one-year deadline to the study of the question. If it were to prolong its study indefinitely, I would not support it. I find it acceptable and I am one of those who support it.

No, Mr. Chairman. It is quite apparent that when the government accepted the strike role for the air division there was no requirement for it to do so in the sense that it was not obliged to do this. It could have declined. In that event it could have left the performance of this duty to others such as, for example, the United States air force. However, the government did not decline the role. It accepted the role. It said that the Canadian air division will undertake the strike role on behalf of the NATO alliance. The reasons for that were fairly obvious. Our NATO allies felt that the air division was the best air division in Europe. It is indeed the best air division in Europe. It is the best trained. It has the best airmen. One of the reasons is, of course, that they are professional. They know what they are doing, and they know it well. Hence an experiment was to be performed whereby on the ground in Europe an air division was to be phased out of the air defence role and into the strike attack role.
This course naturally appealed to the air force. It appealed to the NATO commanders in Europe. The Canadian government was approached with respect to the proposition that Canada would undertake this very difficult and dangerous assignment. The Canadian government accepted the role. The Canadian government must have known at the time when it accepted the role that it involved the use of nuclear weapons, as this matter was implicit in the decision. If the Canadian government accepted this responsibility, knowing in advance that it involved a nuclear commitment, why is there now this indecision with respect to it? The minister, of course, is evading the issue when he says there is no decision with respect to NATO control. There was no decision with respect to NATO control at that time but there was the possibility of
Supply-National Defence a joint arrangement with the United States. Indeed, it was this possibility of joint control with the United States that was referred to by the Prime Minister in this House of Commons when referring to the new role which was to be adopted by the R.C.A.F. and it was subsequently referred to by the former minister of national defence. Having this in mind, Mr. Chairman, surely we must now be assured by the government either that it intends to carry out tests and fulfil its commitment to NATO or that in the meantime it has changed its mind for one reason or another. Otherwise we cannot vote these funds intelligently.

speechtext: Nonsense.

speechtext:
Somebody said "nonsense". Listen to what the Prime Minister said, and see if that is nonsense. It is the basis of this discussion. As the Leader of the Opposition has reminded us, the Prime Minister said in Edmonton:
Should war come, are we going to arm Canadians with bows and arrows?
He was not talking about political war. He was talking about nuclear war involving the destruction of the civilization of the world, the destruction of Canadian men and women as well as our armed forces. That is what the Prime Minister was discussing, yet someone says "nonsense". The questions put to the Minister of National Defence by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Trinity were intended to ascertain whether or not the statement of the

Prime Minister could be implemented under current defence policy and given full effect.
There is no quarrel with the basic statement made by the Prime Minister-"Should war come, are we going to arm Canadians with bows and arrows?". The advent of war is something which we are all working against. Then the Prime Minister went on to say:
Canada has 65 interceptor aircraft which would be more effective with nuclear weapons. The same applies to the two Bomarc anti-aircraft bases being built in this country.
Then, to show the solemnity of the situation he envisaged as being potential, and which he, along with every other civilized man and woman, hopes will never eventuate, he added:
Should war come we must have available the necessary instrument.
That is the eventuality which we are now discussing. The Leader of the Opposition is not engaging at this moment in a discussion of Canada's policy with regard to nuclear weapons. We are not discussing whether or not there has been any conflict between the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to nuclear policy at this time. That is not the subject under discussion. The Prime Minister was talking about the eventuality of war, and in that context he affirmed his belief that our Canadian forces must have available the necessary instruments. And in the context of modern armament developments, the necessary instruments are nuclear weapons. Now, surely, we are entitled to demand from the Minister of National Defence before this item receives the sanction of parliament an answer to the question: how are we to have these necessary instruments made available to us? We asked this question of the minister because these are his estimates and because the Prime Minister is not here tonight to elucidate the statement which he made in this regard. But we have had no reply from the Minister of National Defence. The hon. gentleman keeps saying that this question has been put to him over and over again, and that he has given a reply over and over again. In fact, he has not answered the questions put to him by two hon. members on this side of the committee. He has walked out of this chamber even as this discussion has been going on, and is now standing behind the curtain when he should be in his place addressing himself to the question before us.

I have listened to what you have just said, Mr. Chairman; I am sure you will find that I have no intention of veering from the area of discussion which you think is proper at the moment.
We have had it established that the Prime Minister was visualizing what could happen in the event of a third world war in which nuclear weapons would be used. He suggested -and in my judgment quite properly-that the Canadian armed forces must be equipped with the best possible weapons. We are not talking about nuclear weapons in Canada in the context of the discussion represented by the division of opinion which prevails between the Minister of National Defence and his colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This is not the issue now under discussion. We are simply asking the minister what steps the Prime Minister had in mind when he said we could obtain these weapons as readily as possible. Indeed, he said we could obtain them within a very short time, namely half an hour. We are entitled to an explanation from the minister. As we all know, nuclear weapons now in the control of the United States under the law of that country cannot escape the monopolistic custody of the government of that country or its agents. The question of joint control is a matter which Mr. Rusk said the other day is open to negotiation. That statement suggests that some arrangement could be made between the United States and Canada with regard to the matter of joint control. We are entitled to have from the Minister of National Defence some comment on this phase of the matter. Is that arrangement what is in contemplation? If that arrangement is in contemplation, when does the government propose to take steps to make available within half an hour, as the Prime Minister said, these weapons which he said were essential in order to endow our military forces with the best possible weapons?
Surely this a simple question which even the Minister of National Defence cannot seek to convince us he has not understood. I am sure that he has understood it. I am equally sure that it is his responsibility to tell us

what the answer is. The minister is asking us to vote certain moneys. The minister is not a dictator. He may sometimes act as one, but he is not a dictator. He is a servant of the people. He is a servant of parliament. We have a right to elicit from him this information. He can sit in his seat and refuse to give it. He can look irritated. He can look offended. Those are the privileges of human beings sittings in this House of Commons. However, if he wishes to do his duty he has no right to refuse this information to parliament. If he persists in refusing to give answers to questions which have been asked by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Trinity, then the hon. member for Trinity was justified in saying that the minister is treating this house with contempt. The minister stands in contempt of this house, and as a result he stands in contempt of the Canadian people. The minister has no other course open to him but to answer us or to say that on the grounds of strict security no responses can be given to these questions. That is not the position taken by the Prime Minister. However, if the minister says this, we shall be obliged to consider the position in which we find ourselves. However, that is not the defence that the minister offers. He simply refuses to say anything. That is the position in which we have been placed tonight as a result of this arrogant conduct on the part of this uncommunicative Minister of National Defence.

In editorial comment in many newspapers there appears something like this. This one appeared in a paper not usually unfriendly to the present Conservative administration. I refer to the Timmins daily Press. It is entitled, "Thirty Minutes is Too Long", and reads as follows:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker has at last declared his government's policy on nuclear arms. And what a policy. In a speech in Edmonton at the week end he stated that if war broke out Canadian forces would be armed with nuclear weapons. So Canada will wait until an attack is launched before it even gets the means to fight back.
Asked whether the weapons would arrive fast enough from the United States in the event of war, if Canada didn't already have them, Mr. Diefenbaker said he could not reply for security reasons. He stated, however, that nuclear warheads for Canada's 65 Voodoo interceptors and Bomarc missiles could be made available in 30 minutes or an hour.
This is not a fiction that the opposition is creating, Mr. Chairman. This is an impression which is widespread in the country and which has been reported in other newspapers. Many newspapers have written editorials about it, including many which are friendly to the government. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has so rightly stated, the Prime Minister has introduced a new policy and he has introduced it in the most unlikely of places, outside of the House of Commons in a speech to a Progressive Conservative association meeting in Edmonton.
We have the right to know how this policy was arrived at. We have the right to know whether it is feasible. We have the right to know by what means it may be implemented, and raises many questions which are pertinent to the vote now before us. "Who?" "John." "Who?" "The Prime Minister of Canada. Will you telephone the Prime Minister of Canada and tell him that the war has started and it is time for him to go and get nuclear warheads that he alleges he needs for the defence of Canada?"
There have been those who have said that continental defence in the missile age is a myth, but the minister by inference at least in asking us to spend millions of dollars for continental defence still believes that it is a valid defence posture. If the minister believes it is a valid defence posture, he must believe that the weapons under his control should be armed in their most effective manner. He has told us in times gone by, we were told by the previous minister and we have been told by the Prime Minister as recently as a week or two ago in Edmonton that in order to accomplish this it is necessary for nuclear devices to be employed. Are we to obtain these nuclear devices for our continental defence or are we not? This is the question to which the minister must address himself because if he does not the whole concept of his expenditure in relation to continental defence is just absurd.
If the minister feels as strongly on this subject as we are led to believe he does, if within the cabinet he is in direct conflict with the Secretary of State for External Affairs and if the minister feels it is essential that these weapons should be equipped with nuclear warheads, he should resign from the cabinet and tell the Canadian people what his views really are. That is the honourable course


for him to take. If he does not agree with this waffling policy being followed by the government, let him resign and say so and tell us the basis on which his resignation is to take effect.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has adopted his usual tactics of trying to evade a perfectly reasonable request for information on our part by saying that this item has nothing to do with our request for information. How many times do we have to read the item to him to make him understand that it calls for an expenditure of $31 million for major air equipment? Surely when we are spending this amount of money for major air equipment we have the right to try to find out whether or not that equipment can be used effectively. That is the issue, Mr. Chairman, but the minister says that has nothing to do with the question and that we are not going to talk about general defence policy or anything like that.
Our interest in this matter has been especially aroused by the fact that the Prime Minister has made statements outside the house which bear on the effectiveness or

otherwise of the use of this equipment. It is perfectly certain that when the Prime Minister made his speech in Edmonton he was trying to explain a change of policy on the part of the government by which nuclear warheads would not be obtained at this time for the equipment we are talking about in the committee tonight. But to reassure people like the minister, who had said earlier that this equipment was of no value without such warheads, the Prime Minister went on to make a statement that there was a report that these nuclear warheads could be obtained within half an hour to an hour. This was a report which the Prime Minister referred to in his statement on policy to a Conservative meeting, a very important statement indeed and one which bears directly on this item.
Having made this supplementary statement about the report, he then went on to say there was some credence in this report. The word "credence" means there was some authenticity in the report. There was something in the report which made it believable. If this is the case, and the Prime Minister states that, have we not the right to ask the minister to tell us more about this statement than we have got from him so far?
If in fact this can be done, if in fact the Bomarc squadron at North Bay can be armed, if the government so decided to arm it, with nuclear warheads within an hour, that would be an entirely different situation and would have a very important bearing on our whole defence policy. If the F-101 Voodoos could be armed in that way in an hour that would make a big difference. But we know and the minister knows that this is one of the most absurd statements ever put on the record and we ask the minister to clear it up and to agree that it is an absurd statement.
The fact is, of course, that part of the money we are being asked to vote tonight will no doubt be spent on these Bomarc squadrons. These two squadrons occupy a pretty strategic place in the link of Bomarc squadrons across the continent. Presumably they were put where they are being put, in the Laurentians and at North Bay, to guard the entry into the continent, down through New York state and into the steel area of Pittsburgh and Detroit. If this Bomarc defence has any validity at all-and some of us doubt whether it has any validity at all- but if we are to take the government's position as stated that this is an important element in our defence, then those two squadrons right in the middle of that chain of defence are vital to that defence. They were put there by the Canadian government after
Supply-National Defence consultation with the United States government. They are now there, but they cannot be used because the equipment for that purpose has no ammunition.
We are being asked to vote money for these missiles without knowing whether or not these missiles could be used in an emergency because the government will not make up its mind how they are to be armed. When we keep pressing the minister for information on this vital point, he keeps on saying we are not going to discuss policy tonight; he says to parliament, you have to vote the money and we will later on decide whether or not this equipment can be used. This is the position the government has asked us to accept tonight.

speechtext: The minister said that the first aeroplane had not yet been delivered to the Canadian air division. Not a single aeroplane delivered, nor a decision taken to adopt this aeroplane until I do not know how long ago. In any event, would the minister answer this question. How can you manufacture, turn out and equip an aircraft without knowing what weapons system it is to have?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member had been here between half past four and five o'clock this afternoon he would have heard me say that this particular aircraft will have the capability of carrying eight different types of weapons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: I was here between half past four and five o'clock and I did not hear the minister say that. But that does not answer my question. Are you going to equip an aeroplane for overseas service, knowing that it can have any one of eight different weapons system, and not decide which one you are going to use in the aeroplane?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, I think it is quite evident that you might use different ones at different times, depending on what particular purpose you have in mind.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: Oh.

646. To provide that George Alvin Baycroft, a former employee of Her Majesty, shall, subject to such terms and conditions as the treasury board prescribes, be deemed to have been designated a contributor pursuant to paragraph (f) of subsection (1) of section 4 of the Public Service Superannuation Act on the 1st day of October, 1957, $1.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting to say a word on this vote. I trust I am in order, because this item refers to pensions and other benefits and I want to refer to one or two items mentioned by the Auditor General in his report which was tabled at the end of March.
The report mentioned a 27 year old corporal who was fired as an "administrative nuisance" and granted a life pension worth $27,000. Then the auditor general mentioned that a 37 year old R.C.A.F. officer-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I do not like to interrupt the hon. member but this particular vote has no general application. As is indicated, it is to provide a pension for a member of the department who inadvertently, because of the regulations that existed, did not get a pension. In other words, it is to correct a mistake and
[The Deputy Chairman.]

is to provide a pension for this gentleman who should have been designated by the governor in council to have been a contributor under the superannuation act but, due to an administrative oversight, this was not done. The omission was not discovered until after his retirement and consequently for superannuation purposes under the act his employment ceased on September 30, 1957, whereas in fact it continued until August 31, 1959. This administrative error reduced his public service by one year and eleven months, so that instead of getting the pension to which he was entitled he is receiving a pension of some $12 a month less than he should be getting. This action is taken to correct that administrative omission.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: If I am out of order, I will wait for the main estimates to deal with the question.

Item agreed to.
670. To authorize loans to be made in the current and subsequent fiscal years in respect of housing projects constructed, pursuant to an agreement with the Minister of National Defence, for occupancy by members of the Canadian forces; such loans to be at interest rates and in accordance with such terms and conditions as the governor in council prescribes-further amount required. $5,000,000.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: Will the minister explain this vote?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext:
This is to provide for funds for the construction of housing on a loans basis. We are having constructed several housing projects in connection with which the Department of National Defence puts up the money or makes a loan to the entrepreneur to construct the houses. We agree to maintain occupancy for a certain length of time which varies from one project to another. We lend this money, and in return we have a guaranteed rate of rental which amounts in nearly all cases to approximately the same amount as is charged for permanent married quarters, a sum which varies according to the rank of the individual.
This is a means of getting these houses built without making a capital outlay as far as the department or the government are concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: Is this an addition to the total vote, or is this money intended to be spent on some special project?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext:
It is just an addition. The sum of $22 millions has been authorized so far for this purpose. Housing projects already approved, and those approved in principle, amount to $26,254,000, so we need this extra

amount in order to finance these various housing propositions which are urgently needed and in respect of which approval in principle has already been given.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: In other words, they have been approved on the assumption that parliament would grant this money, because this is March 20 and I presume this money cannot be used for anything in the new fiscal year. Or is this a continuing fund?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: Once the loan has been approved it can be made in the next fiscal year. These projects have been approved within the department and, I think, in most cases by treasury board; but before a number of them can be started there must be parliamentary approval of this extra amount.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: There is one other point, and possibly I can get this cleared up. It may not be very important. Can the minister say whether if there were any loans approved after April 1 there would have to be a new vote for this purpose, or is this a continuing vote of money that could be used?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext: This is a continuing vote. Although $22 million have already been approved for this purpose we are asking for a further $5 million. The amount which has been actually put out so far is only $9,784,000, but a further $16,470,000 has received treasury board approval. In some cases the projects have been started. In others approval has been given by the treasury board. In order to go ahead we need the extra money contained in this vote so as to increase the amount of the loans.
Item agreed to.

657. To deem the election made by the late Emery Leduc on the 16th day of September, 1957 to be valid for all purposes of the Public Service Superannuation Act, notwithstanding that he was not medically examined as required by section 18 of the said act, and to authorize payment of benefits to his widow and children as if he had taken and passed the medical examination so required, $1.

maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext: Could we have an explanation of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext: This is something like the item which was just dealt with by the Minister of National Defence. It affects one individual. An error was made at the time he should have made an election with regard to his past departmental service. There was an omission in that procedure, and consequently his widow and children have been deprived of part of the superannuation allowances to which they would have been entitled had that election been correctly made. There was an error, inasmuch as the deceased did not at the proper time undergo a medical examination as required by section 18 (1) of the Public Service Superannuation Act. The action being taken now will result in a benefit to the widow and the children.

maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext: Is this being made retroactive to the date of the man's death?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL, INCLUDING THE MEDICAL RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext: This is a return of the superannuation contributions rather than a continuing pension. Apparently the amount which was returned was inaccurate. As a result of this non-election the widow and children are entitled only to a refund of his contribution in the amount of $1,100.49.
Item agreed to.
